items.summary: Asset-412 is an internet-facing (IP allowlist) Tier 1 server holding names, national IDs, bank details and pay data for about 410,000 individuals. It supports about 340 customers. Asset-413 holds the same figures, so the two servers likely hold overlapping data, and the counts should not be added.

Asset-413 is a second server with the same data types, record count and customer dependency, so one compromise could expose the full set of records. It is unclear whether the two servers hold the same records or split them.

Firewall blocked about 1.84M connections from non-allowlisted IPs in 12 months. These were background scanning that never reached the service, so they show the internet scanning level and not attacks that got through.
2,150 failed key authentications from allowlisted ranges in 12 months, mostly customer misconfiguration. This is a weak signal of hostile activity.
The IDS raised 14 exploit-signature alerts from allowlisted ranges in 12 months. Each is a probable exploit attempt against the SFTP service or OS, and none succeeded.
No confirmed compromises of these servers in 36 months. This is weak evidence of low frequency, not proof of zero, and the OS only went out of support in January 2026.

On 2026-04-09 a compromised customer network was used to guess keys against these servers. It gave no access and no records were affected. It cost 45 response hours, or $6,750, and needed no customer notification. It shows that the allowlisted-customer-network route is used in practice.

items.summary: The SFTP service is 3 releases behind. Vendor fixes exist but cannot be installed on the unsupported OS, which adds to the exposure.
The allowlist has 9 ranges of /16 or larger. This widens the set of networks that can reach the servers, which raises the chance of an attack coming from an allowlisted range.

The September 2025 external pen test found nothing, but it was run only from a non-allowlisted address and the service was not reachable. It has not been repeated since the OS went out of support, so it says little about the exposure from allowlisted ranges.
9 corporate accounts were compromised by credential phishing in 12 months, all contained before lateral movement. This gives context for the internal-foothold path (path 3).

items.summary: The console gives access to all Nova customer tenant data. It is Restricted, Tier 1, and not internet facing. About 9.5M individuals have records and about 3,100 customers depend on it.
There were 9,400 failed console logins in 12 months. Logs are pulled only on request and nothing alerts on them.
There were 310 account lockouts in 12 months. This shows that guessing attempts are happening and that lockout triggers.
A retrospective review found 3 suspected password-spraying bursts in 12 months, none tied to a successful login. The review was one-off, so coverage is limited.
No unauthorized console logins were confirmed in 36 months. Detection coverage is low, so this is weak evidence that the true frequency is zero.

9 corporate accounts were compromised through credential phishing in 12 months, 2 of them support engineers. All were contained before lateral movement. This shows how often the foothold step happens.
The finding that the console is password-only and not behind SSO is rated High and is in progress. 140 of 220 users have moved to MFA as of September 2026, so exposure is shrinking.
An internal pen test in March 2026 got valid console credentials by password spraying from an internal position in 2 of 3 attempts. The testers then reached tenant data.
Password spraying is a known technique that tries a few common passwords across many accounts. It avoids per-account lockout, which matches exploit path 2.
Valid-account abuse covers the use of phished or reused credentials for initial access. It matches exploit paths 1 and 3.

items.summary: The production cloud account is classified Restricted. It holds time and attendance data for about 3.4 million individuals and supports about 2,300 dependent customers. This sizes secondary loss and confidentiality exposure.
The CI/CD platform holds build definitions and deployment credentials. It is Tier 1 and not internet facing. About 2,300 customers depend on it.

The deployment role has a wildcard admin policy, and the finding has been open and rated High since 2026-04-20. The role used only 23 distinct actions in 90 days out of several thousand permitted, so a scoped policy would cut the exposure without much disruption.
Long-lived access keys 14 months old are stored as pipeline variables. This finding is open and rated High, and it supports the leaked-key path.

In a May 2026 penetration test, a tester with a standard engineer account edited a pipeline definition and gained admin access to production. The single reviewer approved the change without noticing. This shows the one-reviewer control did not stop the attack and that the skill needed is low.

Nine corporate accounts were confirmed compromised through credential phishing in 12 months, and 2 belonged to support engineers. All were contained before lateral movement. This is a base rate for engineer account compromise, which is the first exploit path.
The pipeline definition was changed 1,260 times in 12 months. Each change is a chance for a malicious edit to hide among normal activity and be approved.

The SIEM raised 2 alerts in 12 months for the deployment role being used from outside the pipeline address range. Both were closed as benign engineer testing. This shows the detection works but is not evidence of zero attacks.

items.summary: The benefits integration service holds employee names, dates of birth, dependents and benefit elections for about 780,000 individuals. About 1,100 customers depend on it. It is outbound only.
The provider-hosted legacy API holds the same data, about 780,000 individuals across 1,100 customers. It is internet-facing.
All integration sessions (100%) negotiate TLS 1.0. No network inspection exists on this path, so interception attempts would not be visible. Absence of observed attacks is therefore weak evidence.

An architecture review rated this High and it is still open. It found TLS 1.0 and basic authentication with a shared account, first seen 2026-05-12. These weaknesses are confirmed, with no exploit-probability data.

The provider confirms the legacy API gets no security fixes and is outside its SOC 2 scope. No incidents have been disclosed, which is weak evidence of low frequency. The contract requires breach notification within 72 hours.

items.summary: The asset is a group of 85 workstations classed Restricted and holding customer data extracts. The contents vary, and the inventory gives no record or customer counts.

The web proxy logged 420 uploads to personal cloud storage domains in 30 days from 37 distinct users on these workstations. Upload content is not visible, so these are possible exposure paths and not confirmed losses.

In Nov 2025 a support analyst emailed an extract of 5,100 records to a personal address. It was recovered, and one customer was notified. This is one confirmed loss event on this asset and shows the insider path is real.
The incident cost 47,000 USD in total. That is 180 response hours (27,000 USD at the 150 USD/hour loaded rate) plus 20,000 USD of other direct costs.

The scanner found 212 hardcoded secrets in 41 repositories. 27 high-sensitivity secrets were rotated in August 2026 and 185 remain, so exposure is reduced but still large.
The Internal Audit secrets management review failed. Vault use is voluntary and only 38% of services use it, so the vault is a weak resistance control.

MITRE ATT&CK T1213.003 (Code Repositories) covers adversaries collecting data from internal code repositories. This matches the clone-and-harvest step.
